chunks: "You write a small program, called a kernel, for one thread, and launch it across a grid of thousands or millions of threads.
The hardware groups threads into blocks, assigns blocks to streaming multiprocessors, and splits each block into warps of 32 threads.
A warp is the real unit of execution: the SM fetches and decodes one instruction and all 32 lanes execute it at once on their own data. That's SIMT.
Each SM keeps many warps resident, with their registers all on chip. Every cycle the scheduler picks a warp that's ready and issues its next instruction.
When a warp waits on a memory load, which can take hundreds of cycles, the scheduler just issues from another warp. So latency is hidden by parallelism, not by big caches.
Two things hurt. If threads in a warp take different branches, the warp runs both paths with lanes masked off, so you lose efficiency.

And memory access patterns matter a lot: if the 32 threads read consecutive addresses the hardware merges them into one wide transaction, but scattered addresses become many transactions and bandwidth collapses.
So good GPU code is about keeping warps full, avoiding divergence, coalescing memory and using on-chip shared memory for reuse."
